beads.title: Sign this node's key when registering with a wrapped tailnet-lock auth key
beads.description: A pre-auth key issued for a tailnet whose lock is on is not a plain key: it is the key, the literal separator --TL, a base64 (raw-std, unpadded) SigCredential node-key signature, a '-', and a base64 ed25519 private key whose signing authority that credential delegates. At commit 023255e8a27ec9f6a21d24e3eda21c052ff72af3, tka/sig.go's DecodeWrappedAuthkey cuts the string at --TL and returns the two halves, and every decode failure inside it returns the WHOLE original string with isWrapped false, so a malformed suffix degrades to 'this is a plain key' rather than to an error. control/controlclient/direct.go's doLogin then does two things with the result. It registers with the STRIPPED key -- the part before --TL, which is what control issued and expects to see -- and, when the key was wrapped, it calls tka.SignByCredential(wrappedKey, wrappedSig, tryingNewKey.Public()) to build a SigRotation whose Nested is the supplied credential and whose signature is made by the delegated private key, attaching the result as RegisterRequest.NodeKeySignature. That signature is what makes a brand-new node key trusted under the lock from its first contact, with no human running 'tailscale lock sign'. This repository does neither. ts_control::tokio::register takes auth_key: Option<&str> and sets auth: auth_key.map(RegisterAuth::from), and RegisterAuth is a one-field borrow of that same &str, so the whole wrapped string goes to control as the auth key; the literal --TL appears nowhere in the tree; and RegisterRequest.node_key_signature is modelled in ts_control_serde with Go's own comment on it and is set by no caller. So on a locked tailnet an embedder handed a wrapped key sends control an auth key control did not issue, and in the best case (control tolerating the suffix) registers unsigned -- which is a node its peers, including this fork's own peer_tracker, will refuse. The peer-side half of the lock is complete here: ts_tka's verify_signature accepts Credential-rooted chains and deliberately skips the pubkey == node_key bind for a Credential leaf, because SigCredential leaves Pubkey unused and binding it rejects legitimate credential-provisioned peers. What is missing is the self-signing half, and the pieces exist: NodeKeySignature::sign_rotation builds a rotation wrap, and ts_runtime's tka_sign already signs a Direct signature with the persisted network-lock key and submits it over Noise. The work is the --TL decode plus a rotation wrap whose nested signature is a SUPPLIED credential rather than an inner Direct this tree constructs, wired into the register path so the stripped key and the signature go out together. Port Go's refusals with it, because they are the whole safety of the feature: a key with no --TL is a plain key; a suffix with no '-' delimiter, a suffix half that is not valid unpadded raw-std base64, or a signature blob that does not deserialize all degrade to 'plain key' and register unwrapped rather than failing; and SignByCredential refuses outright when the wrapped signature is not of kind SigCredential ('wrapped signature must be a credential, got %v'), which is the usage refusal to port rather than to infer. See PORTING.md section B.

beads.title: Act on the register response's node-key signature and expiry instructions
beads.description: Control answers a register request with two instructions this repository decodes and drops, so each of them lands here as an unexplained refusal that the caller then retries identically forever. At commit 023255e8a27ec9f6a21d24e3eda21c052ff72af3, control/controlclient/direct.go makes registration a two-shot loop: doLoginOrRegen calls doLogin, and if it returns mustRegen it sets opt.Regen and opt.OldNodeKeySignature from that first call and calls doLogin exactly once more. Two response fields set mustRegen. A non-empty RegisterResponse.NodeKeySignature means 'here is the signature your OLD node key carried; re-sign it for the new one': doLogin returns it, and the second pass runs tka.ResignNKS(persist.NetworkLockKey, tryingNewKey.Public(), opt.OldNodeKeySignature), which unserializes the old signature, returns it VERBATIM when it already covers the key being registered, and otherwise wraps it in a fresh SigRotation signed by this node's network-lock private key; the result goes out as RegisterRequest.NodeKeySignature. tka/sig.go's maybeTrimRotationSignatureChain is the bound that makes repeated wrapping safe -- a rotation chain may name at most 15 previous node keys, because CBOR nesting is capped at 16, and past that the chain is rebuilt from the original Direct leaf forward. RegisterResponse.NodeKeyExpired means the key just offered is expired: Go logs it without PII and returns mustRegen so the second pass generates a fresh node key (moving the current one to OldPrivateNodeKey), and it treats regen=true together with NodeKeyExpired as a contradiction and errors ('weird: regen=true but server says NodeKeyExpired'). Here, classify_register_response in ts_control/src/tokio/register.rs reads exactly three things -- machine_authorized, auth_url and error -- and node_key_signature and node_key_expired are both modelled on RegisterResponse in ts_control_serde and read by nothing in the tree. So both instructions classify as MachineNotAuthorized(None): an unauthorized registration with no interactive URL and no reason, after which the same key is offered again with the same missing signature. The failure this produces is a node that worked yesterday and stops today, on node-key rotation or on a lock that was enabled around it, with nothing in the log naming a cause. The machinery is already present: ts_keys::NodeState carries old_node_key and the register path already logs 're-registering with OldNodeKey set', network_lock_keys is persisted, and its public half already goes out as RegisterRequest.nl_key -- which is precisely the declaration on the strength of which control sends the signature back. The work is the loop, not the crypto: classify the two fields into the existing typed error set, re-sign (ResignNKS) or regenerate, and retry ONCE -- Go's single retry is the behaviour to copy, not an unbounded loop. Test the refusals: an old signature that already covers the key being registered is used verbatim rather than needlessly re-wrapped; a chain at the 15-key limit is trimmed rather than extended; a re-sign failure is logged and registration proceeds WITHOUT a signature, because Go's error path does not abort the register; and regen together with NodeKeyExpired is an error, not a third attempt. See PORTING.md section B.

beads.title: Serve MagicDNS AAAA on control's magicdns-aaaa capability, not on a local flag
beads.description: Whether MagicDNS hands out a peer's IPv6 address is control's decision upstream and an embedder's local boolean here, and the two disagree in both directions. At commit 023255e8a27ec9f6a21d24e3eda21c052ff72af3, ipn/ipnlocal/node_backend.go decides a peer's MagicDNS addresses in one function, magicDNSAddrs, from the peer's addresses plus two flags. The default is deliberately conservative and commented as such: if the peer has an IPv4 address at all, its IPv6 addresses are dropped from the answer, 'as we don't guarantee that the peer node actually can speak IPv6 correctly'. Two things lift it. selfV6Only -- this node has v6 addresses and no v4 -- returns only the peer's v6, because there is nothing else this node could reach. And wantAAAA, set when the SELF node holds the magicdns-aaaa capability (tailcfg/nodecap/nodecap.go: MagicDNSPeerAAAA), keeps the peer's v6 alongside its v4; both magicDNSHostAddrs (the on-demand quad-100 path) and dnsConfigForNetmap test nm.AllCaps.Contains(nodecap.MagicDNSPeerAAAA) for it. Upstream dates the behaviour: capability version 116, 2025-05-05, 'Client serves MagicDNS AAAA if NodeAttrMagicDNSPeerAAAA set on self node'. This node declares 125, so control may set the attribute and expect AAAA to start being served. Here the entire decision is one embedder-set boolean: ts_runtime::magic_dns answers an AAAA question for a tailnet name from DnsView::enable_ipv6, which is ts_control::Config::enable_ipv6 carried through ts_runtime::env -- with it off (the default) a known peer's AAAA returns NoError with an empty answer, and with it on the peer's overlay v6 address is returned. The capability map is not consulted and the string magicdns-aaaa appears nowhere in the tree. Both divergences follow. With enable_ipv6 on and the attribute unset, this node hands out a peer's AAAA beside its A, which Go does only when control asked for it and whose comment says why it otherwise does not. With enable_ipv6 off and the attribute set, control asked for AAAA and gets NODATA. The decision this bead carries is how the two gates combine. The recommended shape is a conjunction: keep the local gate, because it is this fork's own anti-leak decision and is load-bearing -- with IPv6 off the node opens no IPv6 socket, so an AAAA it hands out is an address it cannot then reach -- and add the capability as the second condition, applying Go's default suppression (drop a peer's v6 when that peer also has a v4) when the capability is absent. The selfV6Only arm can be assessed and recorded rather than implemented, since a node with only v6 addresses is not a configuration this fork produces today; say which way you went. Assert the negatives: a peer with only a v6 address is answered under the current rules and must not regress; an AAAA for a tailnet name that resolves to nothing is still NXDOMAIN and is never forwarded upstream, which is an existing anti-leak test; and the capability is read from the SELF node, not from the peer being resolved. Read it beside PORTING.md section A row 133, which is the same subject from the host-OS side. See PORTING.md section B.

beads.title: Scale DERP home selection by control's per-region scores
beads.description: Control's only lever for steering a client off a DERP region it is draining does nothing to this node. At commit 023255e8a27ec9f6a21d24e3eda21c052ff72af3, net/netcheck/netcheck.go's addReportHistoryAndSetPreferredDERP picks the home ('preferred') DERP from latency, a five-minute best-per-region history, and stickiness thresholds -- and before any of that arithmetic it fetches dm.HomeParams().RegionScore() and scales every region's latency by its score. It does so twice and deliberately: once over the smoothed bestRecent map, and again over each region's latency in the current report, because the stored reports are not mutated in place in case the scores change. tailcfg/derpmap.go documents the semantics: a score in (0, 1) makes a region proportionally more preferred, a score above 1 penalises it, a region absent from the map is treated as 1.0, scores of zero or below are ignored (Go's guard is literally 'if score := scores.Get(regionID); score > 0'), a nil map means no change from the previous value, and an empty non-nil map resets every score to 1.0. This repository ports everything around that step and not the step. ts_runtime::control_runner::select_home_region reproduces Go's asymmetric comparison -- the new candidate by smoothed latency, the incumbent by this cycle's raw latency -- its 10 ms absolute threshold, and even its integer oldRegionCurLatency/3*2 in preference to the float form, with the divergence at the exact two-thirds boundary written out in the comment. But DerpMap::home_params and HomeParams::region_score in ts_control_serde/src/derp_map.rs are modelled and read by nothing: ts_netcheck::RegionResult carries an id, a latency, a latency-map key and the connected remote, and select_home_region sees only that. So this node keeps choosing its home region on raw latency and reports the result in NetInfo.PreferredDERP -- the field control reads back to decide where to route the node's traffic -- while ignoring the weighting control attached to the map it sent. The work is small and belongs inside the existing pure function so it stays unit-testable: carry the score map from the decoded DERP map to the selection, and apply it to both the smoothed and the raw sides exactly where Go applies it, leaving the hysteresis arithmetic untouched. The cases to pin are Go's guards rather than the happy path: a score of zero or below is ignored rather than treated as infinitely preferred; a region absent from the map is unscaled; an empty map is a reset and a nil map is not; and a score large enough to move the choice must still clear the same stickiness thresholds, because scoring changes the inputs to the comparison and never the comparison itself. See PORTING.md section B.

beads.title: Answer control's HEAD ping, and stop answering the same ping request twice
beads.description: Control's PingRequest has four arms upstream and one here, and the arm this repository silently drops is the plainest of them. At commit 023255e8a27ec9f6a21d24e3eda21c052ff72af3, control/controlclient/direct.go's answerPing switches on pr.Types. An empty Types is a HEAD ping: answerHeadPing issues an HTTP HEAD to pr.URL under a 15-second timeout and logs the round trip, which is how control establishes that a node is awake and can reach a URL. Types == "c2n" is the control-to-node HTTP request this tree implements. Anything else is a comma-separated list of PingTypes -- disco, TSMP, ICMP, peerapi -- each handed to doPingerPing, with an explicit 'unsupported ping request type: %q' for a name outside that set. Two rules sit around the switch. useNoise := pr.URLIsNoise || pr.Types == "c2n" picks the transport, and a c2n request that did not come out over Noise is REFUSED rather than answered ('refusing to answer c2n ping without noise') unless a debug envknob says otherwise. And the request is only dispatched when isUniquePingRequest agrees: a PingRequest whose URL is empty is bogus and dropped, and a repeat of the previous URL is dropped too, so a re-sent or replayed map response does not produce a second answer. ts_control::handle_ping in ts_control/src/tokio/ping.rs walks ping_request.types and continues past everything that is not PingType::C2N with 'ignoring unsupported ping type'. An empty types list is not an unsupported type but an empty loop, so the HEAD ping is dropped with no log at all -- the least debuggable of the two outcomes. There is no dedup, so every map response carrying a PingRequest is answered however many times control sends the same one. url_is_noise is modelled on the request and read by nothing, which is harmless only because the one arm implemented is the one Go forces onto Noise regardless. And the response is posted to control_url.join(ping_request.url.path()) -- the path only, rebased onto the control URL -- where Go posts to pr.URL as given; that narrowing is defensible and probably worth keeping, but it is currently kept by accident and it drops the query string with it, so it needs a comment either way. The work splits, and the split is the point: the HEAD arm and the isUniquePingRequest dedup are small, self-contained, need no new subsystem and are worth doing first; the doPingerPing arms need a pinger surface this Device does not expose, and its TSMP arm is the send half of the separate 'answer a TSMP ping with a pong' work, so decide those two together and in that order. Carry the refusals: an empty pr.URL is bogus and answered with nothing, a repeated URL is dropped, an unknown type name is logged and skipped rather than failing the whole request, and a c2n request is answered only over Noise. See PORTING.md section B.

beads.title: Send the tailnet-lock head in the map request, instead of a permanent empty string
beads.description: Every map request this node has ever sent tells control that its tailnet-lock chain is at genesis. At commit 023255e8a27ec9f6a21d24e3eda21c052ff72af3, control/controlclient/direct.go keeps the head hash of the local tailnet-lock authority on the Direct client and stamps it into every map request as MapRequest.TKAHead; SetTKAHead reports whether the value actually changed, and control/controlclient/auto.go's Auto.SetTKAHead uses that return to force a fresh map request when it does, so control learns of a local head advance promptly rather than on the next unrelated update. It is the mirror of MapResponse's TKAInfo: control says where it thinks the chain is, and the client says where it actually is. Here, MapRequest::tka_head is modelled in ts_control_serde/src/netmap.rs as &'a str with Go's own description on it, and MapRequestBuilder in ts_control/src/map_request_builder.rs has no setter for it, so it takes its Default and goes out empty on every request. The bound is worth stating so this is not read as worse than it is: this tree's sync is driven entirely from the response side -- ts_runtime::control_runner::maybe_sync_tka compares control's TKAInfo.Head against the local Authority's head and syncs when they differ, which is Go's tkaSyncIfNeeded -- so an empty request-side head costs correctness nothing here, and a node with a lock still syncs. What it costs is honesty on the wire: a control plane that reads TKAHead to decide what to send, or to notice a node whose chain has forked or fallen behind, sees a node permanently at genesis, which is exactly the 'no control plane can distinguish this from a Go client' line this repository is measured against. The work is a setter on the builder fed from the synced authority's head in its base32 form -- Authority::head and AumHash::to_base32, both already used by the sync path -- plus Go's changed-or-not return so that a head advance triggers a map request rather than waiting for one. The negative cases: no synced authority means the empty string, not a zero hash; and an unchanged head must not force a request, or a node with a lock sends map requests in a loop. See PORTING.md section B.

beads.title: Drop NetInfo.HairPinning, a wire field upstream deleted
beads.description: ts_control_serde models a tailcfg.NetInfo field that upstream no longer has. Upstream stopped populating NetInfo.HairPinning in May 2024 (9eb72bb51, #12205) and removed the last symbols in de733c595, 2025-11-09, 'tailcfg: kill off rest of HairPinning symbols' -- the struct field, its Clone, its view accessor and its tests. At commit 023255e8a27ec9f6a21d24e3eda21c052ff72af3 the NetInfo struct in tailcfg/tailcfg.go carries MappingVariesByDestIP, WorkingIPv6, OSHasIPv6, WorkingUDP, WorkingICMPv4, HavePortMap, UPnP, PMP, PCP, PreferredDERP, LinkType, DERPLatency and FirewallMode, and the string HairPinning does not appear anywhere in tailscale/tailscale. ts_control_serde/src/net_info.rs still declares hair_pinning: Option<bool> with the old Go doc comment on it, under skip_serializing_if = "Option::is_none". There is no divergence on the wire today and this bead should say so plainly rather than overstate itself: nothing in this tree sets the field, so it is always None, so it is always absent, which is a field-by-field match with a Go client that no longer has it. What is worth closing is the trap -- the only thing standing between this tree and an identifiable not-a-Go-client tell is that nobody has yet written to a pub field, and a NetInfo carrying a "HairPinning" key is something no Go client has sent since 2024 -- and, more usefully, the audit that found it. The check is mechanical and belongs in the repository rather than in one worker's head: resolve every pub field in ts_control_serde to the wire name it actually serializes under (its #[serde(rename = "...")] if it has one, else the PascalCase of the field name) and look that name up in upstream's Go at the pinned commit; a name upstream does not have is a field this tree models alone. Run at this pin it returns exactly this one field. The work is the deletion plus, if it is cheap, the check itself as a test or a devtool so the next drift is caught by CI instead of by a re-derivation of the parity ledger. Do not remove the neighbouring NetInfo fields while you are there: have_port_map, link_type and the rest all still exist upstream, and the acronym-rename regression test in that module must keep passing unchanged. See PORTING.md section B.

beads.title: Compute Go's three peer display names instead of showing the raw FQDN
beads.description: Where a Go client shows a peer as 'laptop', this repository's status surface shows 'laptop.tailnet-name.ts.net'. At commit 023255e8a27ec9f6a21d24e3eda21c052ff72af3, tailcfg/tailcfg.go's Node.InitDisplayNames computes three fields on the CLIENT, not in control -- the comment above them says so, 'populated from controlclient (not from control)' -- and control/controlclient/map.go and direct.go call it with the netmap's MagicDNS suffix on the self node and on every changed peer. The rule has four steps. Trim the tailnet's MagicDNS suffix from Node.Name, which yields the short base name for an ordinary node and the whole FQDN for a shared-in node whose name sits under a different tailnet. Take dnsname.SanitizeHostname(Hostinfo.Hostname) as the host name and discard it when it equals the base name case-insensitively. If the base name came out empty, promote the host name into it, and fall back to the node key's string form when there is no host name either. Finally build ComputedNameWithHost as 'name (host)' when a differing host name survived and as the bare name otherwise. Node.DisplayName(forOwner) then chooses between the two: the owner of a node sees the disambiguating form, everyone else sees the short one. Here, ts_runtime::status::StatusNode::from_node sets a single field by a single rule -- node.fqdn_opt(false).unwrap_or_else(|| node.hostname.clone()) -- and its test status_node_display_name_prefers_fqdn asserts exactly that. So two peers Go disambiguates as 'laptop' and 'laptop (laptop-2)' both appear here as FQDNs, and a shared-in peer is not distinguished from an ordinary one. Node.ComputedName and Node.ComputedNameWithHost are the only two tailcfg fields with no counterpart in ts_control_serde, which is the same fact from the other side; note they are json-tagged, so control MAY send them, but Go overwrites whatever arrives by calling InitDisplayNames itself, and a port should do the same rather than trusting control. Scope note for triage: this is a status surface only. No peer and no control plane observes it, so it is the lowest-consequence of the open parity rows and should be ranked accordingly; it is filed because ipn/ipnstate is a mapped package and because an embedder reading Device status today gets a different string than tailscale status prints. The work is InitDisplayNames as a function over the domain Node, called where the netmap is ingested rather than at each status read, plus the owner/not-owner choice on the way out. Carry the refusals, because they are the whole of the function: a host name equal to the base name case-insensitively is dropped rather than shown in parentheses, an empty base name promotes the host name instead of rendering empty, and a node with neither falls back to the node key rather than to an empty string. See PORTING.md section B.
